title: Who Pays for AI?
subtitle: The environmental costs of data centers and the choices that distribute them
question: How do choices about power source, cooling, and cost sharing affect the environmental costs of AI data centers and the energy bills of nearby households?
thesis: Responsible AI growth needs technical choices that lower resource use and policy choices that share the remaining costs fairly.

sections.title: Introduction
paragraphs: As an AI answer appears on a screen, there are real buildings and equipment running in the background. Servers use power, cooling systems remove heat, and utilities connect data centers to shared grids. People who use AI may live far from the places that supply these resources. This raises my main driving question: how do choices about power source, cooling, and cost sharing affect the environmental costs of AI data centers and the energy bills of nearby households? My answer is that responsible AI growth needs two kinds of choices: technical choices that lower resource use, and policy choices that share the remaining costs fairly.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data centers used 485 terawatt-hours of electricity worldwide in 2025, and its central projection reaches about 950 terawatt-hours in 2030 [7]. These figures cover all data center services, not just AI. To picture this, 485 TWh equals 485 billion kilowatt-hours, roughly the annual electricity purchases of 45 million US homes, using the 2022 average of 10,791 kWh per residential customer [5]. This is a comparison of scale, not a claim that those homes were deprived of electricity.

This project shows how a data center’s electricity supply, cooling system, and grid upgrade agreement affect resource use and household energy costs in lower and higher income communities. I answer it with a simulation, presented as an interactive website, in which every choice a user has is a simplified assumption. The project also lets users experience Meadows’s idea of leverage points: changing equipment affects resource use, while changing payment rules affects who carries the cost [9]. The model shows relationships between these choices; it does not predict what will happen in a real city.

sections.title: Electricity Use
paragraphs: A data center needs electricity to run its servers and cooling systems. This electricity usually comes from the local grid, which combines power from different types of power plants. Coal and natural gas plants burn fuel to generate electricity, releasing carbon dioxide. Wind turbines use moving air, hydropower uses flowing water, and solar panels convert sunlight into electricity without burning fuel. These sources produce much lower carbon emissions during operation. Lower-carbon electricity therefore means fewer emissions for the same amount of electricity used, not that the data center needs less power. This is why my model separates the amount of electricity from its source. Berkeley Lab estimates that US data centers used 176 terawatt-hours in 2023, or about 4.4 percent of national electricity use, and projects that this could rise to between 325 and 580 terawatt-hours by 2028, with AI servers as a major reason [12]. Since data centers already use a significant share of grid electricity, their choices can affect other users connected to it. The wide range in the projection also shows that the future depends on choices not yet made, which is what my simulation can explore.

Masanet and colleagues’ research gives a different picture of the recent past. From 2010 to 2018, computing in data centers rose about six times even though electricity use grew only about 6 percent, because gains in efficiency offset most of the growth [8]. But I do not think past results mean that today’s AI growth will follow the same path. The gains Masanet describes included more efficient equipment, better utilization, and moving work into larger cloud facilities. Berkeley Lab identifies growing use of accelerated servers as a major driver of rising demand [12]. So Masanet shows us efficiency matters, and Berkeley Lab suggests that efficiency alone may not keep demand flat this time. These studies cover different periods and regions; they are not a single continuous forecast.

These two sources are the foundations for the electricity part of my simulation. I keep computing work fixed and multiply total facility electricity use by an emissions factor. This isolates the effect of the power source instead of guessing how fast AI demand will grow. The calculation follows the basic method in EPA guidance [4]. The two factors I use, 400 and 50 kilograms of CO₂e per megawatt-hour, are examples I chose to represent higher- and lower-carbon supplies. Wind, solar, and hydro illustrate the lower-carbon approach; these coefficients are not measured values for a particular facility. The model does not consider emissions from making hardware, construction, and backup generators, so it covers only part of the environmental cost.

sections.title: Cooling and Water Use
sections.takeaway: A tradeoff between water and power
paragraphs: Cooling is a second environmental cost in addition to electricity, and the two cooling methods in my model trade water for power. Evaporative cooling removes heat as water evaporates; dry cooling transfers heat to air. Mytton separates onsite cooling water from water used to make electricity; my model counts only the former [10]. Dry cooling uses less direct water but more power in my simulation. Research supports this possible tradeoff, but its size is chosen for this example [12].

An air-cooled chiller removes heat without relying on water evaporation. Shehabi and colleagues explain that these systems “employ air-cooled condensers to remove heat from the system” (40). This saves onsite water, but it can require more electricity. As the report states, “While air-cooled chillers use no water, they use more energy” (45) [12]. An evaporative cooling tower, on the other hand, removes heat as some of its water evaporates, creating a need for replacement water. This approach can use less electricity than an air-cooled chiller, but it consumes water. The choice therefore involves a tradeoff between onsite water use and electricity use.

Research on US data centers shows that both location and power supply affect environmental costs [13]. The same amount of water matters more where water is scarce. Because my model leaves out watersheds, seasons, and drought, it reports liters without estimating local water stress. Dry cooling alone does not prove that a data center has no effect on water systems: extra electricity can also require water at power plants, outside this model’s boundary.

Viborillas, a town in Mexico’s drought-prone state of Querétaro, provides a concrete example. In a 2026 report, some residents said they received water only three days a week, while others reported going without it for as long as a month. Resident Rita Zeferino said, “Sometimes we get water, sometimes we don’t” [2]. Residents worried that nearby data centers were worsening shortages, although a local official said water problems existed before the centers arrived. The report does not establish how much of the shortage data centers caused, but it shows why additional industrial water demand raises concerns where families already struggle to meet basic needs.

To keep the numbers and tradeoff easy to follow, the appendix lists the main inputs. Users can change the power source, cooling method, household income, and cost-sharing rule; the other values are chosen by me. The input ledger below presents that appendix for the website.

sections.title: Income and Cost Sharing
sections.takeaway: The same bill. A different burden.
paragraphs: The third element of the model is household budgets, because the same bill has a very different weight for families with different incomes. The American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy defines energy burden as “the percentage of household income spent on energy bills” [3]. This definition is why my model compares lower and higher incomes using the same energy bill: incomes of $30,000 and $100,000 and a yearly bill of $1,800. These are comparison values, not survey results, and keeping the bill the same makes the impact of income easier to see.

One example adds a household perspective. In 2026, News 5 Cleveland followed Keith and Cheryl Kasnik of Perry Township, near a cryptocurrency mining campus. Their monthly electric bill passed $500 in December and $600 in February, and from December through March they paid about 60 percent more for power than a year earlier [6]. The nearby facility was not identified as an AI center, and the report does not establish its share of the increase. For a family earning $30,000, the same dollar increase would be a far heavier burden than for a family earning $100,000; those are my comparison incomes, not the Kasniks’ reported income.

Policies can help protect households from extra costs. Ohio’s tariff requires large new data centers served by AEP Ohio to pay minimum charges based on contracted capacity, even if they use less [11]. In February 2026, AEP Ohio reported 5,642 MW of binding contracts under the tariff, compared with earlier requests for 30,000 MW. The company said financial commitments help avoid unnecessary infrastructure. These new contracts are separate from 12,219 MW contracted before the tariff [1]. The update suggests reduced risk of paying for speculative construction; it does not demonstrate lower household bills or energy burdens.

Therefore, the model offers three choices: the company pays, residents pay, or each pays half. The assumed upgrade costs $20 million, spread over ten years and 10,000 households. This gives annual household charges of $0, $200, or $100, without interest. This choice applies Meadows’s idea of leverage points: changing the rules about who pays can be a stronger place to intervene than adjusting a single payment [9]. These charges recover the modeled grid upgrade, not the facility’s own electricity bill.

sections.title: Results and Limitations
paragraphs: Under its assumptions, the simulation gives three important results. Choosing the low-carbon source reduces electricity emissions to one-eighth of the higher-carbon scenario, an 87.5% reduction, but leaves electricity demand unchanged. Dry cooling cuts onsite water use by about 98% but raises total electricity use by about 12.5%. The $1,800 bill is a 6% burden for the $30,000 household and 1.8% for the $100,000 household; the residents-pay option raises these to about 6.7% and 2.0%. These are calculated examples, not measured outcomes at a real facility.

Each result points back to my argument. A cleaner power source lowers the environmental cost without lowering the demand placed on the grid. Dry cooling moves a cost rather than removing it. And because the model holds the household bill fixed, only the cost-sharing rule changes what households pay. Lower resource use and fair cost sharing are two separate problems, and solving one does not solve the other.

The limits of this model are clear. Its fixed inputs ignore factors such as future growth, changes in equipment use, hot days, and peak demand. The model also does not link the data center’s electricity use to household bills, so the extra power from dry cooling never shows up as a cost to residents. It does not estimate jobs, tax revenue, land impacts, supply chains, or AI’s possible social benefits, so it cannot weigh AI’s gains against its costs or support a full judgment about any real AI data center.

sections.title: Conclusion
paragraphs: My question asked how choices about power, cooling, and cost sharing affect the environmental costs of AI and the costs paid by nearby households. The model’s answer is that these choices affect different problems. A low-carbon power source lowers emissions without lowering electricity demand, and dry cooling lowers direct water use but raises electricity use under these assumptions. A cost-sharing rule decides who pays for the modeled upgrade, and energy burden shows why the same charge matters more to a lower-income household. The Kasniks’ bills and the Ohio tariff show why responsible AI growth needs both: lower resource use protects the environment, and fair cost sharing protects the people living alongside the infrastructure that supports computing.
